title: StepX-OPD: Rethinking Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation in Diffusion Models

paper.title: StepX-OPD : Rethinking Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation in Diffusion Models
paper.abstract: Abstract A deployable text-to-image diffusion model must hold several capabilities at once, such as instruction following, text rendering and human preference, and must sample in a few steps. Capabilities and few-step sampling are built in separate stages: a full-step model first consolidates capabilities through multi-teacher on-policy distillation, then serves as a fixed teacher for step distillation. Every full-step model we evaluate scores lower once compressed, and the second stage cannot begin until the first finishes. We introduce StepX-OPD , which merges the two stages: one student acquires every capability while learning to sample in a few steps, so frozen specialists supervise it on the states its own rollout visits rather than on a longer trajectory it never runs. Because a decomposition of the rollout’s KL weights velocity mismatch most heavily near the clean end, we also regress the student’s velocity on the low-noise part of the rollout. Separately, we find that capability integration makes models write prompt words into images on prompts that never asked for text, and we give a variant that lowers it. We evaluate on SD3.5-Medium and FLUX.1-dev across instruction following, text rendering, image quality and human preference. On both architectures, StepX-OPD attains the highest normalized average score among the four-step methods compared and exceeds the forty-step Flow-OPD model, and on SD3.5-Medium it trains with about 37% fewer GPU-hours than sequential DiffusionOPD followed by step distillation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Flow matching and diffusion models are widely used for text-to-image generation ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) . A model prepared for deployment must meet two needs at once: it must be capable across composition, text rendering, image quality, and human preference, and it must be fast, measured by how few sampling steps its inference requires. Models meet these needs through two separate lines of post-training, one that integrates capabilities into a single model and one that compresses its sampling trajectory into a few steps. These two lines are developed independently, each advancing its own need while leaving the other untouched. Yet both needs are placed on the same deployed model, so capability integration and step distillation constrain that model together. Existing methods address these two deployment needs separately. Capability integration builds on on-policy distillation, which supervises the student on states the student itself generates ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . In continuous image generation, DiffusionOPD ( Li et al., 2026 ) , Flow-OPD ( Fang et al., 2026 ) , and DanceOPD ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) use analytic transition KL or local regression to integrate capabilities, but retain full-step sampling. Step distillation, by contrast, starts from a teacher whose capabilities are already fixed. DMD ( Yin et al., 2024b ) and DMD2 ( Yin et al., 2024a ) use a frozen teacher score and an auxiliary fake-score estimator, while Qwen-Image-Flash ( Wu et al., 2026 ) combines a base teacher with a post-trained teacher. TDM ( Luo et al., 2025 ) , CDM ( Liu et al., 2026b ) , and SenseFlow ( Ge et al., 2025 ) move supervision toward student-generated trajectories or nearby states, which improves the few-step trajectory. These compression methods still treat teacher capabilities as inputs. A multi-capability few-step model therefore continues to rely on a serial pipeline: multi-teacher capability integration first produces a full-step multi-capability model, and step distillation then treats that model as a fixed teacher for few-step compression. The serial pipeline lengthens training, because compression starts only once the full-step capability model finishes. Fig. reports the training cost each optimization stage carries. Beyond this training cost, it leaves open the question: do the capabilities integrated into the full-step model still hold once its sampling trajectory is compressed to a few steps? We test this directly by comparing each full-step capability model with its few-step compressed counterpart: Tab. reports lower aggregate scores for every one of them after compression, with larger declines on individual metrics. Fig. shows that these full-step OPD models already render prompt words into images more often than the base model, on prompts that neither request nor forbid text, before their trajectories are shortened. Transition matching in continuous-image OPD and marginal matching in DMD ( Yin et al., 2024b ) and TDM ( Luo et al., 2025 ) both admit reverse-KL interpretations over different distributions and states. Theorem analyzes this relationship through a reverse-KL decomposition. Motivated by this decomposition, we propose StepX-OPD , which integrates capabilities and compresses sampling in one training run, without an intermediate full-step OPD model. Frozen specialists supervise the student directly on the states its current few-step rollout visits, with each mini-batch going to the specialist for its training source. Because this decomposition weights the low-noise part of the rollout most heavily, StepX-OPD also regresses the student’s velocity there, telling it not only which distribution to land in but also which direction to move. We evaluate StepX-OPD on SD3.5-Medium ( Esser et al., 2024 ) and FLUX.1-dev ( Labs et al., 2025 ) across GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) , OCR accuracy ( Chen et al., 2023 ) , DeQA ( You et al., 2025 ) , PickScore ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) and their normalized Average, against sequential Flow-OPD + TDM and DiffusionOPD + TDM baselines. On both architectures, StepX-OPD achieves the highest Average among the few-step systems, 0.8901 and 0.8902, and exceeds the forty-step Flow-OPD model, and on SD3.5-Medium it trains with about 37% fewer GPU-hours than DiffusionOPD + TDM. On prompts that do not request text, recurrence rises from 21 images for the SD3.5-Medium base to 218 for DiffusionOPD, and StepX-OPD , trained with the DiffusionOPD teachers, reduces it to 94, and to 84 with its precise-teacher variant. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We introduce StepX-OPD , which trains capability integration and few-step compression together on the student’s current rollout, with the routed specialist supplying both the distribution-matching and the velocity-regression targets. • We measure unintended prompt-word rendering on prompts that neither request nor forbid text, find it rises with capability integration, and give a variant that reduces it. • We show under a common protocol that every full-step capability model we evaluate scores lower once compressed, and that StepX-OPD attains the highest Average among the few-step systems on both architectures and, on SD3.5-Medium, trains with about 37% fewer GPU-hours than sequential DiffusionOPD + TDM.

sections.heading: Step distillation.
sections.text: Within distribution-matching methods, DMD uses the difference between real and fake score fields as a reverse-KL gradient. It also adds regression on teacher-generated noise–image pairs, so part of the update still depends on a multi-step teacher sampler ( Yin et al., 2024b ) . DMD2 removes this paired regression, uses two-time-scale updates to stabilize fake-score learning, adds adversarial training, and uses fixed-schedule backward simulation for multi-step students ( Yin et al., 2024a ) . Decoupled DMD separates CFG augmentation from distribution matching and gives them different re-noising schedules, while retaining DMD2’s fixed simulation and fake-score training ( Liu et al., 2026a ) . A data-dependent alternative, Moment Matching, matches conditional clean-data means. SiD derives data-free score identities ( Salimans et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) . TDM instead matches intermediate trajectory marginals over step-dependent intervals, without instance-level trajectory matching ( Luo et al., 2025 ) . SenseFlow adapts DMD to large flow backbones through implicit alignment, intra-segment guidance, real-data supervision, and a VFM discriminator, while keeping coarse fixed anchors ( Ge et al., 2025 ) . CDM replaces fixed anchors with dynamically sampled on- and off-trajectory states. This broadens supervision but adds training-time evaluations, while inference uses the same number of steps ( Liu et al., 2026b ) . Qwen-Image-Flash blends base and reinforcement-trained teacher scores with a fixed step schedule. The selected blend is more stable than its specialist-only setting ( Wu et al., 2026 ) . These methods still provide fixed capabilities to the distillation objective; Qwen’s blend is also fixed in advance rather than chosen from the states the student visits, motivating the on-policy routing methods discussed next.

sections.heading: On-policy distillation in diffusion models.
sections.text: On-policy distillation lets a teacher supervise the states the student visits during generation, rather than states drawn from an offline trajectory or dataset. DiffusionOPD ( Li et al., 2026 ) lifts this idea from the discrete token transitions used in language models to the continuous-state denoising process, modeling each step as a Gaussian transition and deriving a closed-form per-step KL objective in place of a PPO-style surrogate. Flow-OPD ( Fang et al., 2026 ) first trains a domain-specialized teacher per reward with single-reward GRPO, then merges the teachers into a cold-started student via on-policy sampling and task-routing labeling, adding a Manifold Anchor Regularization term in which a task-agnostic teacher anchors generation to a high-quality manifold. DanceOPD ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) treats each frozen capability as a velocity field over the denoising state space, routing each sample to one field, querying it once on a low-noise state from the student’s rollout, and training with a plain velocity mean-squared-error objective. A second arrangement applies on-policy supervision after step distillation rather than before it. D-OPSD ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) tunes an already step-distilled few-step model by having the same network act as teacher and student under different conditioning, the student seeing only the text prompt while the teacher also sees the target image, so it learns new concepts or styles on its rollout without degrading its distilled few-step behavior. Both arrangements treat capability integration and step-count reduction as separate stages; StepX-OPD places multi-teacher on-policy supervision inside the few-step distillation objective, carrying out both in a single stage. For a broader review of unintended text rendering, see App. .

sections.heading: 4 Method
sections.text: StepX-OPD trains one student to carry out multi-teacher on-policy distillation and step distillation at the same time, rather than consolidating capabilities at full step count and compressing the result afterward. We build on trajectory distribution matching (TDM) ( Luo et al., 2025 ) and redraw the rollout grid at random on every training step. Sec. then constructs supervision states between the nodes of that grid, Sec. routes each mini-batch to the frozen specialist that supplies its target velocity, and Sec. regresses the student’s velocity field directly on the low-noise ones. Alg. in App. gives the complete training procedure.

sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental setup
sections.text: Model. We evaluate two base architectures, SD3.5-Medium ( Esser et al., 2024 ) and FLUX.1-dev ( Labs et al., 2025 ) . For each, the joint OPD models and task-specialist teachers use forty-step generation and the step-distilled students, including StepX-OPD , use four steps. Every evaluated model is sampled at 512 × 512 512\times 512 resolution. On SD3.5-Medium, full-step models use a classifier-free guidance scale of 4.5 and four-step students a scale of 1.0. FLUX.1-dev instead carries a distilled guidance embedding, set to 3.5 at forty steps and 1.0 at four steps, with classifier-free guidance disabled throughout. Benchmark. We evaluate each base model, its task specialists, and its joint OPD models at forty steps, together with step-distilled variants of the base and joint OPD models at four steps, on GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) , OCR accuracy ( Cui et al., 2025 ) , DeQA ( You et al., 2025 ) , and PickScore ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) , combined into a single Average score. Tab. reports these four measures and Average for both SD3.5-Medium and FLUX.1-dev under the same protocol, and Tab. additionally reports CLIPScore ( Xu et al., 2024 ) , HPSv2.1 ( Wu et al., 2023 ) , Aesthetic ( Murray et al., 2012 ) , ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) , and UnifiedReward ( Wang et al., 2025 ) for the SD3.5-Medium rows, outside the Average score. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: Multi-capability, few-step text-to-image models are typically built in two stages: a full-step model consolidates capabilities, then serves as a fixed teacher for compression. This lengthens training, and the capabilities gathered in the first stage do not fully survive into the second. StepX-OPD merges the two stages, learning capabilities directly on the few-step trajectory the deployed model runs and removing the intermediate full-step teacher. A reverse-KL decomposition characterizes this supervision and motivates velocity regression on the trajectory’s low-noise part. Capability integration also leads models to render prompt words into images on prompts that neither request nor forbid text, and we give a variant of StepX-OPD that reduces this behavior. Evaluated on SD3.5-Medium and FLUX.1-dev, StepX-OPD reaches the highest Average among the four-step methods on both and exceeds the forty-step Flow-OPD, and on SD3.5-Medium it trains with about 37% fewer GPU-hours than sequential DiffusionOPD followed by step distillation.

sections.heading: Appendix C Evaluation protocol
sections.text: For every evaluated model, we generate four images for each GenEval record, OCR prompt, and PickScore prompt. See Sec. for the sampling steps, guidance scale, and resolution used to generate them. GenEval’s 2,212 records cover 553 unique strings. The resulting image counts are 8,848 for GenEval, 4,072 for OCR, and 8,192 for PickScore. DeQA and the five additional measures that Tab. reports are evaluated on the same fixed 250-image subset from each of GenEval, OCR, and PickScore, for 750 images total. GenEval uses the official detector-based scorer; OCR uses normalized target-string matching with PaddleOCR; and PickScore is reported both in its raw scale and, when forming Average, after division by 26. sections.heading: Text rendered without being asked for.
sections.text: Work that touches this behavior reaches it from several directions. On the representation side, Materzyńska et al. (2022) show that CLIP’s image encoder holds spelling and scene content in one space, and that text-to-image methods guided by CLIP spell out the single word they are conditioned on, in a setting where generation is an iterative optimization through CLIP rather than a trained sampler. SpectralCLIP ( Xu et al., 2024 ) names these written words textual artifacts and suppresses them by masking the frequency band of the CLIP embedding they occupy, a remedy that acts on the CLIP guidance path a flow matching sampler does not pass through. Censored sampling ( Yoon et al., 2023 ) treats the behavior as something to remove at sampling time: Stable Diffusion, asked for a photo of a human, sometimes produces prominent embedded text or shows text in place of any human figure, and about 23.7% of the samples drawn from that one hand-written prompt are judged malign, which ties the measurement to the prompt rather than to a benchmark a model is scored on. TangPoetryBench ( Hu et al., 2026 ) instead scores it under prompts that instruct the model to include no text, giving text integrity a dimension of its own that separates leakage of the prompt’s own text from garbled characters and counting 119 of 1,280 images as carrying a text issue, so what it measures there is disobedience of an explicit instruction. On the reinforcement learning side, DDPO ( Black et al., 2024 ) reports a policy trained against a vision-language reward printing the string sixx ttutttas over an image of eight turtles, presented as one qualitative case from a single-reward run, and RLRF ( Rodriguez et al., 2025 ) lists a text-in-image hack in which the policy emits the prompt string as an SVG text primitive rather than drawing the described scene. Hong et al. (2026) organize the failure modes of text-to-image reinforcement learning around artifact-prone generation and train an artifact reward model as a regularizer for the reward models in use, and rendered text is not among the modes that catalogue lists. Flow-OPD ( Fang et al., 2026 ) attributes degraded aesthetics under aggressive optimization of text rendering to reward hacking, citing Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , and the evidence it reports for the effect is a drop in GenEval, which reads object composition rather than what the image writes. We report this behavior as a count taken under one protocol on benchmark prompts that neither ask for rendered text nor forbid it, on the same backbone before and after several rewards are integrated into it.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY-SA 4.0 arXiv:2611.04386v1 [cs.CV] 03 Nov 2026 StepX-OPD : Rethinking Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation in Diffusion Models Chenru Wang Xuanyang Zhang Yucheng Han Affiliation: StepFun Wenbo Nie Wei Cheng Affiliation: StepFun Xianfang Zeng Affiliation: StepFun Gang YU Affiliation: StepFun Chi Zhang Affiliation: Westlake University GitHub | | Hugging Face | | Project Page Abstract A deployable text-to-image diffusion model must hold several capabilities at once, such as instruction following, text rendering and human preference, and must sample in a few steps. Capabilities and few-step sampling are built in separate stages: a full-step model first consolidates capabilities through multi-teacher on-policy distillation, then serves as a fixed teacher for step distillation. Every full-step model we evaluate scores lower once compressed, and the second stage cannot begin until the first finishes. We introduce StepX-OPD , which merges the two stages: one student acquires every capability while learning to sample in a few steps, so frozen specialists supervise it on the states its own rollout visits rather than on a longer trajectory it never runs. Because a decomposition of the rollout’s KL weights velocity mismatch most heavily near the clean end, we also regress the student’s velocity on the low-noise part of the rollout. Separately, we find that capability integration makes models write prompt words into images on prompts that never asked for text, and we give a variant that lowers it. We evaluate on SD3.5-Medium and FLUX.1-dev across instruction following, text rendering, image quality and human preference. On both architectures, StepX-OPD attains the highest normalized average score among the four-step methods compared and exceeds the forty-step Flow-OPD model, and on SD3.5-Medium it trains with about 37% fewer GPU-hours than sequential DiffusionOPD followed by step distillation. 1 1 footnotetext: Work done during an internship at StepFun. 2 2 footnotetext: Project lead. 3 3 footnotetext: Corresponding author. Figure 1: Training cost for the displayed optimization stages (left) and four-step performance across nine benchmarks after fixed axis-wise normalization (right). 1 Introduction Flow matching and diffusion models are widely used for text-to-image generation ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) . A model prepared for deployment must meet two needs at once: it must be capable across composition, text rendering, image quality, and human preference, and it must be fast, measured by how few sampling steps its inference requires. Models meet these needs through two separate lines of post-training, one that integrates capabilities into a single model and one that compresses its sampling trajectory into a few steps. These two lines are developed independently, each advancing its own need while leaving the other untouched. Yet both needs are placed on the same deployed model, so capability integration and step distillation constrain that model together. Existing methods address these two deployment needs separately. Capability integration builds on on-policy distillation, which supervises the student on states the student itself generates ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . In continuous image generation, DiffusionOPD ( Li et al., 2026 ) , Flow-OPD ( Fang et al., 2026 ) , and DanceOPD ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) use analytic transition KL or local regression to integrate capabilities, but retain full-step sampling. Step distillation, by contrast, starts from a teacher whose capabilities are already fixed. DMD ( Yin et al., 2024b ) and DMD2 ( Yin et al., 2024a ) use a frozen teacher score and an auxiliary fake-score estimator, while Qwen-Image-Flash ( Wu et al., 2026 ) combines a base teacher with a post-trained teacher. TDM ( Luo et al., 2025 ) , CDM ( Liu et al., 2026b ) , and SenseFlow ( Ge et al., 2025 ) move supervision toward student-generated trajectories or nearby states, which improves the few-step trajectory. These compression methods still treat teacher capabilities as inputs. A multi-capability few-step model therefore continues to rely on a serial pipeline: multi-teacher capability integration first produces a full-step multi-capability model, and step distillation then treats that model as a fixed teacher for few-step compression. The serial pipeline lengthens training, because compression starts only once the full-step capability model finishes. Fig. reports the training cost each optimization stage carries. Beyond this training cost, it leaves open the question: do the capabilities integrated into the full-step model still hold once its sampling trajectory is compressed to a few steps? We test this directly by comparing each full-step capability model with its few-step compressed counterpart: Tab. reports lower aggregate scores for every one of them after compression, with larger declines on individual metrics. Fig. shows that these full-step OPD models already render prompt words into images more often than the base model, on prompts that neither request nor forbid text, before their trajectories are shortened. Transition matching in continuous-image OPD and marginal matching in DMD ( Yin et al., 2024b ) and TDM ( Luo et al., 2025 ) both admit reverse-KL interpretations over different distributions and states. Theorem analyzes this relationship through a reverse-KL decomposition. Motivated by this decomposition, we propose StepX-OPD , which integrates capabilities and compresses sampling in one training run, without an intermediate full-step OPD model. Frozen specialists supervise the student directly on the states its current few-step rollout visits, with each mini-batch going to the specialist for its training source. Because this decomposition weights the low-noise part of the rollout most heavily, StepX-OPD also regresses the student’s velocity there, telling it not only which distribution to land in but also which direction to move. We evaluate StepX-OPD on SD3.5-Medium ( Esser et al., 2024 ) and FLUX.1-dev ( Labs et al., 2025 ) across GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) , OCR accuracy ( Chen et al., 2023 ) , DeQA ( You et al., 2025 ) , PickScore ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) and their normalized Average, against sequential Flow-OPD + TDM and DiffusionOPD + TDM baselines. On both architectures, StepX-OPD achieves the highest Average among the few-step systems, 0.8901 and 0.8902, and exceeds the forty-step Flow-OPD model, and on SD3.5-Medium it trains with about 37% fewer GPU-hours than DiffusionOPD + TDM. On prompts that do not request text, recurrence rises from 21 images for the SD3.5-Medium base to 218 for DiffusionOPD, and StepX-OPD , trained with the DiffusionOPD teachers, reduces it to 94, and to 84 with its precise-teacher variant. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We introduce StepX-OPD , which trains capability integration and few-step compression together on the student’s current rollout, with the routed specialist supplying both the distribution-matching and the velocity-regression targets. • We measure unintended prompt-word rendering on prompts that neither request nor forbid text, find it rises with capability integration, and give a variant that reduces it. • We show under a common protocol that every full-step capability model we evaluate scores lower once compressed, and that StepX-OPD attains the highest Average among the few-step systems on both architectures and, on SD3.5-Medium, trains with about 37% fewer GPU-hours than sequential DiffusionOPD + TDM. 2 Related work Step distillation. Within distribution-matching methods, DMD uses the difference between real and fake score fields as a reverse-KL gradient. It also adds regression on teacher-generated noise–image pairs, so part of the update still depends on a multi-step teacher sampler ( Yin et al., 2024b ) . DMD2 removes this paired regression, uses two-time-scale updates to stabilize fake-score learning, adds adversarial training, and uses fixed-schedule backward simulation for multi-step students ( Yin et al., 2024a ) . Decoupled DMD separates CFG augmentation from distribution matching and gives them different re-noising schedules, while retaining DMD2’s fixed simulation and fake-score training ( Liu et al., 2026a ) . A data-dependent alternative, Moment Matching, matches conditional clean-data means. SiD derives data-free score identities ( Salimans et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) . TDM instead matches intermediate trajectory marginals over step-dependent intervals, without instance-level trajectory matching ( Luo et al., 2025 ) . SenseFlow adapts DMD to large flow backbones through implicit alignment, intra-segment guidance, real-data supervision, and a VFM discriminator, while keeping coarse fixed anchors ( Ge et al., 2025 ) . CDM replaces fixed anchors with dynamically sampled on- and off-trajectory states. This broadens supervision but adds training-time evaluations, while inference uses the same number of steps ( Liu et al., 2026b ) . Qwen-Image-Flash blends base and reinforcement-trained teacher scores with a fixed step schedule. The selected blend is more stable than its specialist-only setting ( Wu et al., 2026 ) . These methods still provide fixed capabilities to the distillation objective; Qwen’s blend is also fixed in advance rather than chosen from the states the student visits, motivating the on-policy routing methods discussed next. On-policy distillation in diffusion models. On-policy distillation lets a teacher supervise the states the student visits during generation, rather than states drawn from an offline trajectory or dataset. DiffusionOPD ( Li et al., 2026 ) lifts this idea from the discrete token transitions used in language models to the continuous-state denoising process, modeling each step as a Gaussian transition and deriving a closed-form per-step KL objective in place of a PPO-style surrogate. Flow-OPD ( Fang et al., 2026 ) first trains a domain-specialized teacher per reward with single-reward GRPO, then merges the teachers into a cold-started student via on-policy sampling and task-routing labeling, adding a Manifold Anchor Regularization term in which a task-agnostic teacher anchors generation to a high-quality manifold. DanceOPD ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) treats each frozen capability as a velocity field over the denoising state space, routing each sample to one field, querying it once on a low-noise state from the student’s rollout, and training with a plain velocity mean-squared-error objective. A second arrangement applies on-policy supervision after step distillation rather than before it. D-OPSD ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) tunes an already step-distilled few-step model by having the same network act as teacher and student under different conditioning, the student seeing only the text prompt while the teacher also sees the target image, so it learns new concepts or styles on its rollout without degrading its distilled few-step behavior. Both arrangements treat capability integration and step-count reduction as separate stages; StepX-OPD places multi-teacher on-policy supervision inside the few-step distillation objective, carrying out both in a single stage. This lengthens training, and the capabilities gathered in the first stage do not fully survive into the second. StepX-OPD merges the two stages, learning capabilities directly on the few-step trajectory the deployed model runs and removing the intermediate full-step teacher. A reverse-KL decomposition characterizes this supervision and motivates velocity regression on the trajectory’s low-noise part. Capability integration also leads models to render prompt words into images on prompts that neither request nor forbid text, and we give a variant of StepX-OPD that reduces this behavior. Evaluated on SD3.5-Medium and FLUX.1-dev, StepX-OPD reaches the highest Average among the four-step methods on both and exceeds the forty-step Flow-OPD, and on SD3.5-Medium it trains with about 37% fewer GPU-hours than sequential DiffusionOPD followed by step distillation.
